requirements: The core contributions of the two-stage GPU kernel tuner combining semantic refactoring and search-based optimization have been reproduced.

sub_tasks.requirements: The hardware, software, and model environment used in the paper is available and configured for reproducing all experiments.
The GPU hardware environment matches the paper's specification (NVIDIA TITAN RTX, single machine).

Code has been implemented to detect and verify that experiments run on an NVIDIA TITAN RTX GPU (via nvidia-smi, torch.cuda.get_device_name, or equivalent), and the reproduction script logs the detected device name.
Code has been implemented to verify that a single-GPU execution mode is used (no multi-GPU / distributed configuration) so that timing measurements are not skewed by cross-device coordination.

Code has been implemented that queries and records the hardware resource upper-bound vector r(h) (SM count, max threads per block, shared memory per block, registers per SM, warp size) used by the tuning agent to derive the feasible parameter space on the TITAN RTX (Turing, compute capability 7.5).
The CUDA / PyTorch software stack required to build, run, and benchmark SGLang kernels is installed and reproducible.

Code has been implemented (setup script, requirements.txt/environment.yml, or Dockerfile) that pins a CUDA toolkit version compatible with TITAN RTX (compute capability 7.5), an nvcc compiler, and a PyTorch version supporting fp16/bf16/fp32 tensor operations, and the reproduction pipeline is runnable from this environment specification.

Code has been implemented to build the CUDA kernels (SGLang baseline, Astra outputs, and templated outputs) as PyTorch extensions (via torch.utils.cpp_extension or a Ninja-based build), and the build succeeds on the configured environment without errors.
Code has been implemented that fixes random seeds and cuDNN/CUDA determinism flags so that generated input tensors and correctness comparisons are reproducible across runs.
The LLM backing all four agents is configured as DeepSeek-V3.2 (deepseek-chat) uniformly across the pipeline.

Code has been implemented to configure the DeepSeek API (endpoint, API key, and model identifier `deepseek-chat` corresponding to DeepSeek-V3.2) as the shared LLM backend for the planning, generation, tuning, and testing agents.

The reproduction verifies at runtime that all four agents (planning, generation, tuning, testing) use the same base model (`deepseek-chat` / DeepSeek-V3.2), so that comparisons against Astra are attributable to the method rather than model differences.

Code has been implemented to handle DeepSeek API failures (timeouts, rate limits, transient errors) with retries and logging, so the multi-round agentic loop can complete without silently skipping iterations.
GPU measurement conditions are controlled so that timing results are stable and comparable to the paper.

Code has been implemented that performs GPU warm-up prior to any measurement and inserts torch.cuda.synchronize() (or cudaDeviceSynchronize) around timing regions, ensuring measurements exclude cold-start effects and asynchronous launch latency.

Code has been implemented that, at experiment start, verifies GPU is otherwise idle (no competing processes) and optionally sets a fixed application clock / persistence mode via nvidia-smi, so per-shape runtimes reported in Figures 2-5 and Table 1 are reproducible on the TITAN RTX.
The three baseline CUDA kernels (silu_and_mul, fused_add_rmsnorm, merge_attn_states) from SGLang are extracted and runnable as the baseline reference.
The SGLang source repository providing the three CUDA kernels is obtained and made available to the tuning pipeline.
Code has been implemented to acquire the SGLang repository (via clone or vendored copy) at a version that contains all three target CUDA kernels (silu_and_mul, fused_add_rmsnorm, merge_attn_states).
Code has been implemented to pin and record a specific SGLang commit / release tag so the extracted baseline kernels are reproducible across runs.
Kernel1 (silu_and_mul) from SGLang is extracted as an independently compilable and runnable baseline CUDA kernel.
Code has been implemented such that the SGLang silu_and_mul CUDA kernel source (device function + launch wrapper) is extracted into the project as a standalone module.
The extracted Kernel1 baseline supports both fp16 and bf16 input tensors as required by the evaluation setup.
Code has been implemented providing a host-side launcher for Kernel1 that accepts (n, h, d)-shaped inputs, allocates device buffers, invokes the SGLang kernel, and returns the output tensor.
Kernel2 (fused_add_rmsnorm) from SGLang is extracted as an independently compilable and runnable baseline CUDA kernel.
Code has been implemented such that the SGLang fused_add_rmsnorm CUDA kernel source is extracted into the project as a standalone module preserving its fused add + RMSNorm semantics.
The extracted Kernel2 baseline runs on fp32 tensors of shape (m, n) as specified for evaluation.
Code has been implemented providing a host-side launcher for Kernel2 that handles the input tensor, residual tensor, and RMSNorm weight and invokes the SGLang kernel end-to-end.
Kernel3 (merge_attn_states) from SGLang is extracted as an independently compilable and runnable baseline CUDA kernel.
Code has been implemented such that the SGLang merge_attn_states CUDA kernel source is extracted into the project as a standalone module.
The extracted Kernel3 baseline supports both fp16 and bf16 input tensors as required by the evaluation setup.
Code has been implemented providing a host-side launcher for Kernel3 that accepts (m, n)-shaped attention state tensors and invokes the SGLang merge kernel to produce the merged output.
The three extracted SGLang kernels are compilable and executable as a single baseline library usable by downstream components.

Code has been implemented providing a build/compile script (e.g., nvcc invocation or setuptools/CMake target) that produces a working binary/library exposing all three baseline kernels on the target CUDA toolchain.
Each extracted SGLang kernel runs without crashing on at least one representative input shape from its evaluation set and produces a finite output tensor.

Code has been implemented exposing a uniform reference-kernel API (e.g., run_baseline(kernel_id, inputs) -> output) used by the correctness verification and performance measurement stages as the SGLang reference S_ref.
The measured baseline runtimes of the extracted SGLang kernels match the values reported in Table 1.

The measured SGLang baseline runtime for Kernel1 (silu_and_mul), aggregated over the reported shapes on an NVIDIA TITAN RTX using the paper's 20-warmup / 100-repetition protocol, matches the reported 199.15 µs.
The measured SGLang baseline runtime for Kernel2 (fused_add_rmsnorm), aggregated over the reported shapes using the paper's measurement protocol, matches the reported 163.76 µs.
The measured SGLang baseline runtime for Kernel3 (merge_attn_states), aggregated over the reported shapes using the paper's measurement protocol, matches the reported 45.83 µs.
The test cases with the specified input shapes and data types for each kernel are constructed and used for correctness and performance evaluation.
The Kernel1 (silu_and_mul) test suite is constructed with the specified 5 shapes under fp16 and bf16 data types.
Code has been implemented that enumerates the five Kernel1 input shapes as (n, h, d) tuples: (512, 32, 256), (512, 40, 128), (768, 32, 256), (768, 40, 128), and (512, 64, 128).
Code has been implemented that instantiates Kernel1 test inputs under both fp16 and bf16 data types for each of the 5 shapes, producing 10 total (shape, dtype) test cases.

Code has been implemented that allocates Kernel1 input tensors with shape and layout matching the SGLang silu_and_mul kernel signature so that both the reference and candidate kernels can be invoked on identical inputs.
The Kernel2 (fused_add_rmsnorm) test suite is constructed with the specified 8 shapes under fp32.

Code has been implemented that enumerates the eight Kernel2 input shapes as (m, n) tuples: (128, 4096), (256, 4096), (1024, 4096), (2048, 8192), (128, 11008), (256, 13824), (512, 14336), and (1024, 8192).
Code has been implemented that instantiates Kernel2 test inputs exclusively under the fp32 data type for each of the 8 shapes.
Code has been implemented that allocates all input buffers required by fused_add_rmsnorm (input, residual, weight) with shapes consistent with the SGLang kernel signature.
The Kernel3 (merge_attn_states) test suite is constructed with the specified 5 shapes under fp16 and bf16 data types.
Code has been implemented that enumerates the five Kernel3 input shapes as (m, n) tuples: (16, 4096), (32, 5120), (32, 8192), (16, 12288), and (64, 8192).
Code has been implemented that instantiates Kernel3 test inputs under both fp16 and bf16 data types for each of the 5 shapes, producing 10 total (shape, dtype) test cases.
Code has been implemented that allocates all merge_attn_states input tensors (attention state prefixes/suffixes and LSE arrays) with shape and layout matching the SGLang kernel signature.
The test-case generation utilities produce reproducible, deterministic, and correctly-typed input tensors suitable for both correctness and performance measurement.
Code has been implemented that seeds all random tensor initializations so that identical inputs are supplied to the SGLang reference and every candidate kernel across a run.
Code has been implemented so that input tensors are materialized in GPU device memory with the requested dtype and contiguous memory layout before invoking the kernels.

Code has been implemented that exposes a unified test-case iterator/loader mapping each kernel (Kernel1, Kernel2, Kernel3) to its full list of (shape, dtype) cases used by both the correctness verifier and the performance measurement loop.
The test-suite composition is consistent with the counts reported in the paper.
The constructed Kernel1 test suite yields exactly 5 distinct shapes evaluated under 2 data types (fp16, bf16).
The constructed Kernel2 test suite yields exactly 8 distinct shapes evaluated under fp32 only.
The constructed Kernel3 test suite yields exactly 5 distinct shapes evaluated under 2 data types (fp16, bf16).
The four-agent closed-loop system (planning, generation, tuning, testing) has been implemented as specified in Section 3.2 with Algorithm 1.
The overall four-agent orchestration and Algorithm 1 control flow are implemented as a runnable pipeline.

Code has been implemented that defines four distinct agent components/classes/modules corresponding to PlanningAgent, GenerationAgent, TuningAgent, and TestingAgent, each with the interfaces described in Section 3.2.

Code has been implemented for a top-level driver that accepts as inputs a baseline kernel S0, target hardware h with resource upper-bound vector r(h), a distance metric d and tolerance epsilon, a searchable parameter vector theta in Theta, and the number of semantic rounds R, matching the Input section of Algorithm 1.
Code has been implemented that returns the tuple (S_tilde*, theta_gen*, D_spec*, Log) as specified in Algorithm 1's Output.

Code has been implemented that performs initialization steps 1-5 of Algorithm 1: constructing test set T from S0, fixing S_ref = S0, initializing S_prev, m_prev, Log, and incumbent best (S_tilde*, theta_gen*, D_spec*) with score* = +infinity.
Code has been implemented for an outer iteration loop that runs exactly R rounds (r = 0 to R-1) executing Level 1 semantic refactoring followed by Level 2 parameter search each round.
Code has been implemented that, at the end of each round, updates S_prev <- S_r and m_prev <- m_r, so subsequent rounds consume the previous round's code and measurement signals.

Behavioral check: running the pipeline on a trivial baseline kernel with R=1 executes all four agents in the order Planning (skipped at r=0) -> Generation -> Testing -> Generation.Templatize -> Tuning -> Testing (evaluate/collect), producing a non-empty Log entry.
The PlanningAgent orchestrates the global optimization: proposes semantic-level suggestions, scores rounds, and selects across rounds.
Code has been implemented for PlanningAgent.Suggest(m_prev) that consumes previous-round measurement signals and returns semantic-level rewriting suggestions g used to guide the GenerationAgent.
Code has been implemented for PlanningAgent.Score(perf_r) that returns the negative geometric-mean speedup as the round's score, as noted in the comment on Algorithm 1 line 27.

Code has been implemented that at each round compares score_r to score* and, when score_r < score*, updates the incumbent best (S_tilde*, theta_gen*, D_spec*) <- (S_tilde_r, theta_gen_r, D_spec_r) and score* <- score_r (Algorithm 1 lines 28-30).

Code has been implemented for the PlanningAgent to centrally manage the objective function and per-round budget constraints, coordinating switching/termination between semantic-level and parameter-level optimization.
Code has been implemented that maintains a versioned repository/log of artifacts (candidate code, templates, configurations, results) enabling traceable and reproducible iteration.
Behavioral check: at r=0 the PlanningAgent.Suggest is NOT invoked and S_r <- S_prev, matching the else-branch of Algorithm 1 lines 8-12.
The GenerationAgent performs semantics-preserving rewriting and templatization exposing tunable parameters.
Code has been implemented for GenerationAgent.Rewrite(S_prev, g) that produces a semantics-preserving rewritten kernel S_r guided by planning suggestions g (Algorithm 1 line 10).

Code has been implemented for GenerationAgent.Templatize(S_r, theta) that converts a candidate kernel into a parameterizable template S_tilde_r with explicitly exposed tunable options and constraint rationales (Algorithm 1 line 17).

Behavioral check: the rewritten kernel S_r and templatized kernel S_tilde_r are emitted as source-code artifacts to disk / the artifact repository each round so that downstream compilation and inspection are possible.
The TuningAgent derives a hardware-feasible parameter space, performs per-input search, and selects general and specialized configurations.
Code has been implemented for TuningAgent.DeriveFeasibleSpace(S_tilde_r, h, r(h)) that returns Theta_feasible_r respecting hardware resource limits (Algorithm 1 line 18).
Code has been implemented for TuningAgent.Search(S_tilde_r, x, Theta_feasible_r) that, for each x in T, returns theta_r*(x) minimizing runtime under constraints (Algorithm 1 lines 19-21).
Code has been implemented for TuningAgent.SelectGeneral({theta_r*(x)}_{x in T}, S_tilde_r, T) that returns a single deployable general configuration theta_gen_r (Algorithm 1 line 22).
Code has been implemented for TuningAgent.BuildSpecialized({theta_r*(x)}_{x in T}, T) that returns a shape-specialized configuration table D_spec_r (Algorithm 1 line 23).
Code has been implemented that submits Top-K tuned candidates from the TuningAgent to the TestingAgent for re-testing and convergence decisions, as described in Section 3.2.

Behavioral check: candidate configurations that would produce compilation failures, invalid launches, or violate resource caps are pruned from Theta_feasible_r before search rather than being executed.
The TestingAgent constructs tests, validates correctness under tolerance, and measures performance/collects signals.
Code has been implemented for TestingAgent.GenerateTests(S0) that constructs the finite test set T used throughout the pipeline (Algorithm 1 line 1).

Code has been implemented for TestingAgent.Validate(S_r, S_ref, T, d, epsilon) that returns pass_r by checking element-wise mismatch against S_ref under metric d and tolerance epsilon (Algorithm 1 line 13).
Code has been implemented for TestingAgent.EvaluatePerformance(S_tilde_r, theta_gen_r, D_spec_r, S_ref, T, h) that returns runtime and speedup measurements perf_r (Algorithm 1 line 24).

Code has been implemented for TestingAgent.CollectSignals(S_tilde_r, theta_gen_r, D_spec_r, T, h) that gathers profiling/measurement signals m_r used to guide the next PlanningAgent.Suggest call (Algorithm 1 line 25).
Closed-loop feedback: correctness gating with rollback, per-round logging, and measurement-driven semantic rewriting.
Code has been implemented that, when pass_r is False, rolls back S_r <- S_prev before templatization proceeds, matching Algorithm 1 lines 13-15.
Code has been implemented that appends a tuple (r, S_r, S_tilde_r, theta_gen_r, D_spec_r, pass_r, perf_r, m_r) to Log every round (Algorithm 1 line 26).
Code has been implemented so that measurement signals m_r collected by the TestingAgent are the input to the next-round PlanningAgent.Suggest, closing the measurement-driven semantic-rewriting loop.
Behavioral check: if a candidate produces mismatched outputs beyond epsilon, it is excluded from becoming the incumbent best and does not overwrite S_prev for the next round.

Behavioral check: across a multi-round run, the Log contains exactly R entries (one per round) and the returned (S_tilde*, theta_gen*, D_spec*) corresponds to the round with the minimum score* (equivalently, maximum geometric-mean speedup).
Model backend configuration for all agents.
Code has been implemented that configures all four agents to use the same base LLM, deepseek-chat (DeepSeek-V3.2), as stated in Section 4 Model choice.
The semantic-level rewriting stage that produces semantics-preserving candidate kernels guided by planning-agent suggestions has been implemented.
The PlanningAgent's semantic-level suggestion mechanism (Suggest(m_prev) in Algorithm 1 line 9) is implemented.

Code has been implemented that exposes a PlanningAgent.Suggest(m_prev) function/method taking measurement signals from the previous round and returning a semantic-level rewriting suggestion object or string.
Code has been implemented so that Suggest is only invoked when r>0 (Algorithm 1 lines 8-11); for r=0 the semantic rewriting step is bypassed and S_r is set to S_prev.

Code has been implemented so that the measurement signals m_prev produced by the TestingAgent (execution times, correctness, performance observations) are passed as input to PlanningAgent.Suggest, driving suggestions from measurement feedback rather than heuristics alone.

The PlanningAgent uses the shared DeepSeek-V3.2 (deepseek-chat) base model to produce semantic suggestions, with a prompt that specifies the goal of proposing semantics-preserving execution-strategy rewrites (parallel granularity, memory-access organization, reduction structure) given the prior kernel and its measurement signals.
The GenerationAgent's Rewrite(S_prev, g) operation performing semantics-preserving structural rewriting is implemented.
Code has been implemented that exposes a GenerationAgent.Rewrite(S_prev, g) function returning a new candidate kernel S_r obtained by applying suggestion g to the previous kernel S_prev.

The Rewrite operation is implemented on top of the deepseek-chat (DeepSeek-V3.2) model, sending both the previous kernel source and the planning suggestion g into the prompt and parsing the returned CUDA kernel source.

The Rewrite prompt/instructions explicitly restrict changes to strategy-family rewrites (execution strategy and resource organization) and forbid altering operator semantics or the kernel's mathematical function, as described in Section 3.2's 'Generation agent' role and the conclusion.
Code has been implemented that extracts a compilable CUDA kernel source (with matching kernel signature to S_ref) from the LLM response and stores it as S_r for downstream validation.
The semantic reference kernel S_ref used to gate all candidates is fixed at initialization.
Code has been implemented that sets S_ref = S_0 (the original SGLang kernel) once at the start of the pipeline (Algorithm 1 line 2) and never mutates S_ref across rounds.

Code has been implemented that initializes S_prev = S_0 and m_prev = empty before the iteration loop (Algorithm 1 line 3), and updates S_prev to the current-round S_r at the end of each iteration (Algorithm 1 line 31).
The Level-1 correctness gate that filters semantically invalid rewrites is implemented.
Code has been implemented that calls TestingAgent.Validate(S_r, S_ref, T, d, epsilon) immediately after the Level-1 rewrite (Algorithm 1 line 13) and stores the boolean result pass_r.
Code has been implemented so that when pass_r is False the pipeline rolls back by setting S_r := S_prev (Algorithm 1 line 14) before proceeding to the Level-2 templating stage.
The correctness gate is executed before GenerationAgent.Templatize is called, ensuring that only semantically valid (or rolled-back) kernels enter the Level-2 templating stage.
The outer semantic-refactoring iteration loop over R rounds is implemented as in Algorithm 1.

Code has been implemented that runs a for-loop for r = 0..R-1 (Algorithm 1 line 6) executing the Level-1 rewrite + gate followed by the Level-2 templating/tuning per round, with R exposed as a configurable parameter.

Code has been implemented that appends a per-round record (r, S_r, S_tilde_r, theta_gen_r, D_spec_r, pass_r, perf_r, m_r) to Log after each iteration (Algorithm 1 line 26), enabling traceable and reproducible optimization.

Code has been implemented that maintains the incumbent-best (S_tilde*, theta_gen*, D_spec*) with score* initialized to +infinity and updated whenever score_r < score*, using the negative geometric-mean speedup as the score (Algorithm 1 lines 27-30).
Behavioral guarantees of the Level-1 stage on the finite test set T are met.

For every kernel S_r that leaves the Level-1 stage (either because pass_r is True, or after rollback to S_prev), the outputs on all x in T match S_ref within the configured tolerance epsilon under the chosen distance metric d.

The Rewrite step only alters execution strategy and resource organization (e.g., loop structure, memory access, threading) and does not modify the kernel's declared inputs/outputs, signature, or numerical operator definition; this is verified by an automated check on the diff between S_prev and S_r (e.g., signature/argument-list equality).

All three final kernels emitted by the Level-1 stage (over all rounds) pass consistency checks against the original SGLang implementations within the configured numerical tolerance, matching the paper's correctness claim in Section 5.1.
The template-based parameterization stage exposing thread-level parallel granularity, loop scheduling/unrolling, vectorization/alignment, and shared memory/register organization is implemented.
The Templatize routine (Algorithm 1, line 17) that converts a semantics-refactored kernel Sr into a parameterizable template S̃r is implemented as part of the GenerationAgent.

Code has been implemented that exposes a GenerationAgent.Templatize(Sr, θ) function taking a source kernel and a parameter vector schema and returning a parameterized template source suitable for downstream feasible-space derivation.

Code has been implemented so that Templatize is only invoked on kernels that passed the semantic correctness gate (or the rollback substitute), preserving the semantic reference throughout templatization.

Code has been implemented that restricts templatization to execution-strategy parameters only (thread-level parallel granularity, loop scheduling/unrolling, vectorization/alignment, and shared memory/register organization), without altering algorithmic semantics of the kernel.

The generated template exposes tunable options via named, interpretable parameter placeholders (e.g., compile-time constants, template arguments, or macros) so that TuningAgent.Search can substitute concrete values without regenerating the kernel from scratch.

Code has been implemented so that Templatize records, for each exposed parameter, a machine-readable rationale/constraint (e.g., which hardware resource limit governs it) that the TuningAgent later consumes in DeriveFeasibleSpace.
The four categories of tunable execution-strategy dimensions described in Section 3.3 are each explicitly exposed by the templating mechanism.
Thread-level parallel granularity dimensions (e.g., block/grid dimensions, elements-per-thread, warps-per-block, tile sizes) are exposed as tunable template parameters on all three target kernels.
Loop scheduling and unrolling parameters (e.g., unroll factor, chunk size along the reduction/element dimension, #pragma unroll factors) are exposed as tunable template parameters.
Vectorization and alignment parameters (e.g., vector width such as float2/float4/half2/half8, alignment assumptions, use of vectorized loads/stores) are exposed as tunable template parameters.

Shared memory and register organization parameters (e.g., shared memory tile size/bank layout, per-thread register buffer size, use/absence of shared memory staging) are exposed as tunable template parameters.

Code has been implemented so that no algorithm-changing or numerics-changing options (e.g., alternative reduction formulas, alternative activation approximations) are exposed as tunable parameters through the templating stage.
Kernel-specific templatization is implemented for each of the three SGLang kernels so that the parameter dimensions above are surfaced appropriately for that kernel's computation pattern.
A templatized version of silu_and_mul (Kernel1) is implemented that exposes at minimum elements-per-thread, block size, vector width, and unrolling as tunable parameters.

A templatized version of fused_add_rmsnorm (Kernel2) is implemented that exposes at minimum block size, elements-per-thread, vectorized load/store width, and shared-memory reduction organization as tunable parameters.

A templatized version of merge_attn_states (Kernel3) is implemented that exposes at minimum thread-level parallel granularity, vector width, and register/shared-memory organization for the state merge as tunable parameters.
Behavioral checks that the templating stage functions correctly are in place.

Instantiating the produced template with any parameter assignment drawn from the declared discrete candidate sets yields a compilable CUDA kernel (no syntactic or preprocessor errors) on the target hardware.

Instantiating the template with a parameter assignment that reproduces the default configuration yields outputs equivalent (under the correctness tolerance ϵ) to the pre-template semantic reference Sr for all shapes in the test set T.

Varying any single templated parameter (e.g., vector width or unroll factor) while holding others fixed produces measurable runtime differences on at least one input shape, demonstrating that the parameter is actually wired through to generated code and not a no-op.
The parameter-selection policy that keeps only a small, broadly applicable set of key dimensions and avoids blow-up of the search space is enforced.

Code has been implemented so that the number of exposed tunable parameter dimensions per kernel template is bounded (small key set) rather than exhaustively enumerating every possible source-level knob, matching the paper's stated design in Section 3.3.

Code has been implemented so that only execution-strategy parameters (not algorithmic-level rewrites) are surfaced at the templating stage, keeping semantic-level changes routed exclusively through the Level-1 semantic refactoring path.
The parameter-level tuning stage — deriving the hardware-feasible search space, searching configurations, and producing general and specialized configurations — is implemented.
The feasible-parameter-space derivation (DeriveFeasibleSpace) that prunes templated parameter combinations against target hardware limits is implemented.

Code has been implemented that exposes a `TuningAgent.DeriveFeasibleSpace(template, h, r_h)` entry point taking a parameterized kernel template, a target hardware descriptor `h`, and a resource upper-bound vector `r(h)`, and returning a set/iterable of concrete parameter assignments Theta_feasible.

Code has been implemented that queries or receives target-hardware resource limits (registers per thread, shared-memory per block, max threads per block, warp size, max blocks per SM) for the NVIDIA TITAN RTX and exposes them as the resource upper-bound vector r(h) consumed by feasibility derivation.

Code has been implemented that enumerates the Cartesian product of discrete candidate values for the exposed template parameters (thread-level parallel granularity, loop scheduling/unrolling factors, vectorization/alignment strategy, shared-memory/register organization) before applying feasibility pruning.

Code has been implemented that prunes combinations violating block-size / thread-count launch limits (e.g., threads-per-block exceeding the device maximum or non-multiples of warp size where required) from the candidate set.
Code has been implemented that prunes combinations whose estimated shared-memory-per-block or register-per-thread usage exceeds the hardware upper bounds encoded in r(h).

Code has been implemented that prunes vectorization/alignment settings incompatible with the tensor dtype and problem-shape alignment (e.g., disallowing vector widths that do not divide the innermost dimension for the given dtype).
Code has been implemented that filters out configurations that fail template instantiation or compilation (nvcc / driver launch failures) so that they are excluded from Theta_feasible before search.

Given a templated kernel and TITAN RTX resource limits, DeriveFeasibleSpace produces a strictly non-empty Theta_feasible for each of the three target kernels (silu_and_mul, fused_add_rmsnorm, merge_attn_states) and no returned configuration triggers a compile-time or launch-time failure when instantiated.
The per-shape search procedure that minimizes runtime under correctness and hardware constraints (TuningAgent.Search) is implemented.

Code has been implemented that provides `TuningAgent.Search(template, x, Theta_feasible)` which, given a template, an input shape x, and the feasible parameter set, returns the configuration theta*(x) minimizing measured on-device runtime.
Code has been implemented that compiles and executes each candidate configuration on-device to obtain empirical runtime measurements used as the search objective.
Code has been implemented that iterates the search over every input shape x in the test set T (per Algorithm 1 lines 19-21) and records theta*(x) for each shape.

Code has been implemented that runs correctness validation (element-wise comparison against the SGL reference within tolerance) for every candidate configuration encountered during search and discards configurations that fail.

Code has been implemented that ranks measured candidates and returns the Top-K configurations to be submitted to the testing agent for confirmation re-tests, matching the tuning-agent behavior described in Section 3.2.

Code has been implemented that enforces a controlled tuning budget (e.g., maximum number of candidate evaluations, wall-clock limit, or explicit search-strategy termination) so that the search cost is bounded as described in Section 3.3.

For each of the three kernels and each specified input shape, the search procedure returns a theta*(x) whose measured runtime is no worse than the SGLang baseline runtime for that shape after correctness gating.
Production of the deployable general configuration and specialized configuration table (SelectGeneral / BuildSpecialized) is implemented.

Code has been implemented that provides `TuningAgent.SelectGeneral({theta*(x)}_{x in T}, template, T)` returning a single general configuration theta_gen intended to maximize average performance across the shapes in T.

Code has been implemented such that SelectGeneral chooses theta_gen by evaluating candidate configurations (e.g., configurations from the pooled per-shape theta*(x) set or Theta_feasible) on every shape in T and picking the one with the best aggregate cross-shape score (mean speedup or geometric-mean speedup vs. SGLang).
Code has been implemented that provides `TuningAgent.BuildSpecialized({theta*(x)}_{x in T}, T)` returning a mapping D_spec from each input shape x in T to its per-shape best configuration theta*(x).

Code has been implemented that serializes theta_gen and D_spec (e.g., as JSON/YAML in the artifact log with the round index) so results are reproducible and consumable by the testing agent for EvaluatePerformance.

For each of the three target kernels, the produced D_spec contains one entry per specified input shape (5 for Kernel1, 8 for Kernel2, 5 for Kernel3) and each entry is a valid, correctness-passing configuration in Theta_feasible.
Integration of the parameter-level stage into the Algorithm 1 iterative loop with logging and best-artifact tracking is implemented.

Code has been implemented that, within each iteration r of the R-round outer loop, invokes DeriveFeasibleSpace, per-shape Search, SelectGeneral, and BuildSpecialized in the order given by Algorithm 1 lines 18-23.
Code has been implemented that appends to the iteration Log a record containing (r, S_r, tilde{S}_r, theta_gen_r, D_spec_r, pass_r, perf_r, m_r) after each round, matching Algorithm 1 line 26.

Code has been implemented that updates the incumbent best (tilde{S}*, theta_gen*, D_spec*) whenever the current round's negative geometric-mean-speedup score is lower than the best-so-far, per Algorithm 1 lines 27-30.

Code has been implemented that skips the parameter-search stage (or rolls back to the previous template) when correctness gating (pass_r = False) fails, so infeasible templates do not corrupt theta_gen* / D_spec*.
Code has been implemented that surfaces the returned (tilde{S}*, theta_gen*, D_spec*, Log) as the final output of the tuning pipeline for downstream reporting (Table 1, Figures 2-4, Figure 5).
The testing agent's correctness gating with element-wise comparison against SGLang under tolerance is implemented and applied to all candidate configurations.
Element-wise comparison infrastructure between candidate kernel outputs and SGLang reference outputs is implemented.
Code has been implemented that runs the candidate GPU kernel and the reference SGLang kernel on the same input tensor and returns both output tensors for comparison.
Code has been implemented that performs element-wise comparison between candidate and reference output tensors (e.g., using torch.allclose or equivalent absolute/relative tolerance check).
The comparison uses a configurable numerical tolerance epsilon appropriate for the tensor dtype (fp16, bf16, fp32), with looser tolerance for half-precision types than for fp32.

The correctness check returns a boolean pass/fail status along with diagnostic information (e.g., max absolute error, max relative error, count of mismatched elements) usable as feedback for the planning agent.
Correctness gating is integrated as a mandatory filter for candidate configurations during tuning.
Code has been implemented that invokes the correctness validation on every candidate configuration produced by the tuning agent's search, before any performance measurement is recorded as final.
Candidate configurations that fail the correctness check are excluded from the feasible set and from the selection of general/specialized best configurations.

Reported final correctness outcomes match the paper's claims.

The benchmarking function executes exactly 20 warm-up runs before starting timed measurements, and the warm-up runs are excluded from the reported runtime.
After warm-up, the benchmarking function executes exactly 100 timed repetitions of the kernel and returns the arithmetic mean of the per-run times as the kernel runtime.
Code has been implemented that uses CUDA events (or an equivalent GPU-side timer) with device synchronization around the timed region to obtain accurate per-run GPU timings.

The benchmarking function is deterministic in structure: given identical inputs and kernel, repeated invocations produce runtimes that are stable enough (low variance across trials) that the 100-run mean is used as the reported single measurement without additional smoothing.

The planning agent's scoring function uses the negative geometric-mean speedup as the score to be minimized when selecting the incumbent best across rounds.
